original_value: According to the FAIR guiding principles, one of the central attributes for maximizing the added value of information artifacts is interoperability. In this paper, I discuss the importance, and propose a characterization of the notion of Semantic Interoperability. Moreover, I show that a direct consequence of this view is that Semantic Interoperability cannot be achieved without the support of, on one hand, (i) ontologies, as meaning contracts capturing the conceptualizations represented in information artifacts and, on the other hand, of (ii) Ontology, as a discipline proposing formal meth- ods and theories for clarifying these conceptualizations and articulating their representations. In particular, I discuss the fundamental role of formal ontological theories (in the latter sense) to properly ground the construction of representation languages, as well as methodological and computational tools for supporting the engineering of ontologies (in the former sense) in the context of FAIR.

result.paraphrase: Drawing on the FAIR guiding principles, this paper argues that interoperability is a key attribute for maximizing the added value of information artifacts. It presents a characterization of Semantic Interoperability and explains that, on this view, it cannot be achieved without (i) ontologies, understood as meaning contracts that capture the conceptualizations embodied in information artifacts, and (ii) Ontology, the discipline that offers formal methods and theories for clarifying those conceptualizations and articulating their representations. The paper also highlights the essential role of formal ontological theories, in this latter sense, in grounding the construction of representation languages, as well as the methodological and computational tools that support ontology engineering, in the former sense, within the FAIR context.
